# A Note on AI Assistance {.unnumbered}

Every chapter of this book was researched, written, and rewritten by me. I also used AI tools throughout. What follows is more than the disclosure MIT Press requires of authors who use AI. It is an honest statement of how AI assisted in navigating fleet-scale systems engineering, and the rigorous human verification standard applied to the result.

This book addresses the engineering required to coordinate thousands of accelerators into a single distributed machine. In developing this text, I used AI tools heavily to build and refine the computational infrastructure that underpins the chapters. This involved extending the [MLSysIM](https://mlsysbook.ai/mlsysim) infrastructure modeling engine from single-node execution to the fleet level: modeling 3D parallelism (tensor, pipeline, and data parallel strategies), collective communication fabrics, cluster network topologies, and fault-tolerance protocols. AI helped write the executable Python cells embedded in the text, implement automated pre-commit checks, and conduct exhaustive surveys across a vast and rapidly moving literature.

Yet mechanical computation and literature synthesis are only the starting point. The most critical and time-intensive phase of writing this book was human validation. To ensure that the analytical models reflect the reality of warehouse-scale computing rather than idealized abstractions, I conducted extensive one-on-one review meetings with domain experts: distributed systems researchers, ML fleet operators, and hardware architects. In these sessions, we walked through chapters, stress-tested assumptions, scrutinized performance equations, and debated design trade-offs. This human feedback loop is perhaps the longest and most demanding part of the authoring process, but it is indispensable. Without that expert review, a systems book risks teaching clean abstractions that fail on real silicon.

Authorship is thinking. Deciding which abstractions belong in the curriculum; determining how to sequence cluster-level concepts so that distributed synchronization is clear before fault tolerance is introduced; choosing which worked examples to trace end-to-end—these are judgment calls that require knowing the reader and the discipline. I used AI as a force multiplier for literature synthesis and simulation code; human experts and I ratified every architectural claim.

This pattern is older than the present moment. In 1683 Joseph Moxon printed the first English-language manual on printing, *Mechanick Exercises on the Whole Art of Printing*, using the press it described. Three centuries later Donald Knuth wrote *The TeXbook* in TeX. A book about machine learning systems infrastructure, written without the infrastructure it describes, would be a contradiction. The toolmaker documents the tool with the tool.

Machine learning systems cannot be certified the way deterministic logic can. That verification gap applies to AI-assisted authoring with equal force. The standard held here is the standard we must demand of every fleet we build: **the tool can propose, but only the human engineer can ratify and take responsibility.**
